questions.q: What is Zehner's main criticism of wind power?
a: Making and moving turbines takes lots of conventional energy
Wind is not actually a renewable resource
Turbines produce too little electricity to matter
Turbines are banned in most countries
questions.why: Lesson 1 says turbine production and transport use so much energy that the carbon footprint can match fossil fuels.

questions.q: Why does hydrogen not solve the transportation problem?
a: Making hydrogen fuel needs more energy than the cell provides
Hydrogen cars emit more CO2 than gasoline cars
Fuel cells are too small to power a car
Hydrogen cannot be stored in a vehicle
questions.why: Lesson 1 says refrigeration and high pressure make hydrogen production extremely energy-hungry.

questions.q: What does the Jevons Paradox describe?
a: Efficiency gains can raise total energy use, not lower it
Economic growth always reduces energy demand
Energy prices fall when supply increases
New technology replaces old technology completely
questions.why: Lesson 2 says more efficient engines made coal cheaper and more popular, so use rose.

questions.q: Why does the author say energy reduction ideas get ignored?
a: They cannot be sold, so they do not fit a productivist economy
They are too expensive for governments to enforce
People do not understand how they work
They have been proven ineffective in practice
questions.why: Lesson 2 says an economy focused on producing and selling things cannot commercialize using less.

questions.q: Which measure does the summary credit with holding California's energy use flat?
a: Cost penalties on products that require heavy energy use
A tax on household income and savings
Subsidies for new wind and solar farms
A ban on building new factories
questions.why: Lesson 3 says California's penalties on energy-heavy products kept per-capita use stable.
